Franklin Delano Roosevelt's first inauguration. On March 4, 1933, exactly four years after Herbert Hoover's last day in office, FDR took the oath at the lowest point of the Great Depression. Unemployment stood near 25 percent, and the banking system was collapsing. His inaugural address struck a note of defiant hope with a single phrase that would define the era: "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." Roosevelt promised aggressive executive action to combat the emergency. He called for broad executive power to wage war against economic crisis, and he warned Congress directly: if they refused to act, he would seek the broad executive power that would be granted if the nation were invaded by a foreign enemy. Over one hundred thousand people gathered on the National Mall, one of the largest inauguration crowds to that date, gathering in hope and desperation. Roosevelt blamed the Depression's severity on the selfishness of financial and banking leadership, signaling that his New Deal would represent an unprecedented expansion of federal power and executive action that would reshape American government for generations to come.
